sections.text: Lord Shri Krishna replied: O Prince! He who shuns not the Quality which is present, and longs not for that which is absent;
He who maintains an attitude of indifference, who is not disturbed by the Qualities, who realises that it is only they who act, and remains calm;

Who accepts pain and pleasure as it comes, is centred in his Self, to whom a piece of clay or stone or gold are the same, who neither likes nor dislikes, who is steadfast, indifferent alike to praise or censure;

We had been discussing chapter 14, Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga, Yoga of the three gunas. So far in Bhagavad Gita, you have learned about ourselves in the first six chapters -- who we are as limited beings, how we function, how we can make the most out of our actions, and how we can be most efficient. And we learned that working without any attachment or expectation is actually the best method to gain the most out of your life and most out of your actions. To become the most proficient and efficient, the basic requirement is not to get too attached to whatever you are doing. This is completely contrary to what we think.
We think the more passionate I am, the better I will be. Bhagavad Gita says its the other way around. The less you are attached to what you are doing, the more efficient you would be, the more successful you would be. So this is what we learned in the first six chapters. Thats called Karma Yoga. How to act in this world as a limited being and to get the most out of your life is Karma Yoga.
Then we focused on who you are in reality -- that you are not this body, you are not this mind, you are not this intellect. So Dhyana Yoga, contemplating upon that supreme self -- the self that I am beyond this limited self -- we have learned this in the next set of chapters, culminating in Bhakti Yoga, the devotion to that self. Unless I identify with something higher, I cannot detach from the lower. To resign from my job, I have to find another job before I resign. If Im a smart person, I dont resign before getting the next job.
You have to find a better job before you can resign from your current one, which you either hate or at least dont love as much. This limited self, even though Im comfortable -- its not the best situation Im in. Im not always happy, Im not always achieving what Im trying to achieve. So Im trying to see something better than what I have today, something which can give me permanent happiness. Bhagavan said, identify with that self which is capable of giving you permanent happiness. Thats Bhakti Yoga.
Bhakti Yoga is truly to identify with that which has no limitations. As long as Im identified with this limited being, there is no chance, ever in eons to come, that Ill achieve my goal of being perfectly happy. But once you identify with that supreme self -- then the question becomes, what is the difference between the limited self and the higher self, and how to go beyond those limitations? So the last chapter we talked about Kshetra-Kshetrajna Vibhaga Yoga.
What is the field and who is the knower? The knower is always someone other than the field. If I know something, that means its an object. If I know my limited self, the limited self is an object, and I, the knower, am knowing the limited self. So there we identified that this body -- Idam Sareeram Kaunteya Etat Kshetram Iti Abhidhiyate -- this body is the field.
This body includes all my experiences, my mind, my thoughts, modifications of my moods -- all that is the field. But one who is witnessing it is the witness. So now, how do I go beyond this? We have been learning in this chapter what is binding this unlimited self to the limited self. And we came to the conclusion that it is the three gunas of the Prakriti. This Prakriti, the manifest world, has three basic qualities.
The three ingredients which make it a pluralistic world, now projecting as a plural world. We know from science that there was nothing but singularity before the Big Bang, and then this world of cosmos came into existence. I was just reading Stephen Hawking -- some dialogue with somebody. And somebody asked him, so what was before the Big Bang?
And he said, nothing. Nothing before the Big Bang. But there was something -- because, as we say, something cannot come out of nothing. So there was something, but that something was not as divided as we perceive it right now. We also learned about cause and effect.
That effect can be nothing but the cause modified. This cosmos cannot be anything but the singularity modified. So Bhagavan said that you have to understand what is binding you to this worldview of pluralistic world. And you are at the center of your own world. Im in the center of my world. Everything relates to me.
If I remove myself from this world, the world disappears. When Im not there, that world does not exist. Whats happening in Syria right now does not exist for me, because Im not there. But whats happening here -- Im very much involved, it all relates to me. Once I remove this limited self out of this equation, the pluralistic world does not exist.
These three gunas are binding this infinite to this limited self. Gunas as we have learned, also means ropes. These three ropes are binding you to this limitedness. We are not giving up our limitedness, but expecting infinite happiness, unlimited existence. We all think that we are going to exist forever. We have learned in Mahabharata that Yaksha asked you this direct question.
What is the most wonderful you find about human beings? The most wonderful, most amazing thing is that everyone knows hes going to die. But they all live like theyre never going to die. We cannot think about ourselves as non existing. Existence is my real nature. But I also know that this life as I know will end sooner or later.
How can I get out of this fear of mortality, this fear of unhappiness? Bhagavan said, you need to get rid of these three binding ropes. You have this great wealth of Sat, Chit, and Ananda, but you just dont have the password to that account. Somebody says, Rajan, your great grandfather left great wealth in a Swiss account -- the only problem is we dont have the account number. So we know that we are Satchitananda.
We just dont know the key to it. So Bhagavan said, know that these three are binding you. Once you get out of these three, you will achieve that state where you are immortal, always blissful, and all-knowing. So we have learned that these three gunas are binding -- they are Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas. Sattva binds you with happiness, Rajas by activity, and Tamas by laziness or inactivity.
So the ultimate prescription was Guna tita Bhava -- go beyond these three gunas. Arjuna obviously says, okay, all this is well and good, but how can one get to that point? The last verse we have seen says Kair lingais trin gunan etan atito Bhavati prabhu -- how can anyone go beyond these three gunas? Once he achieves that, what will be his behavior? Katham cha etan trin gunan ativartate.
How can I understand that this is possible? Give me some indications -- like a litmus test -- that if I see this, it means that person has gone beyond the three gunas. And also, if that is possible, if somebody has already done that, then tell me the recipe for how to get there. Now we know that Bhagavan has been talking about it throughout the Bhagavad Gita. But Arjuna one more time asks this question to make it very clear that this is the goal of life.
So Bhagavan answers in the following verses, and its really very unique. Verse 22 -- this is something we really want to contemplate. What is his answer? Prakasham cha Pravritim cha Moham eva cha Pandava Na dveshti sampravrittani -- he did not say that these gunas will disappear once you become Nirguna, Gunatita. He does not hate when these three gunas are present. Prakasham cha Pravritim cha Moham -- these are the effects of these three gunas.
Prakash -- light, knowledge, clear-headedness. We clearly understand whats going on. Things are very clear, no confusion. Thats the effect of Sattva. When my mind and intellect are in Sattva Guna, everything is crystal clear. I dont need somebodys advice.
I know what is right and what is wrong. Pravritti -- activity, Im busy. Thats the effect of Rajas. And Moha -- delusion. I dont understand whats going on, I dont know whether theyre right or wrong. Moha is the effect of Tamas.
When these are present in my personality, in my mind, I dont hate them. Up till now we were thinking that when somebody says Guna Tita Bhava, it means I will not have those gunas at all. Bhagavan makes it very clear: these gunas will remain as they are. Just because you became Sthita Prajna, the world is not going to change. Neither the quality nor the nature of your body, mind, and intellect are going to change.
If I am a weakling, its not overnight going to change just because I have become a Gnani. The body will have its own Dharma -- it will be exactly what it was before realization and after realization. The mind will have its own Dharma. It has been with you for eons; it has its own personality.
Its not going to change. Neither is the intellect overnight going to become Einstein. We know these are my equipment and I have to live with their limitations. But I, at the core of my being, seeing that happening in my mind and intellect, remain a witness. And I dont hate that. Why am I in this mood? is not a question. This is how I react when things happen this way.
This is my nature. Na nivrittani kankshati -- he also does not desire them when they are not present. When I am in a sattvic mood, things are very clear, and Im very happy about my own clarity. Then when I lose that sattvic mood and get into Rajasic or Tamasic territory, I hate that -- I want to be back to my serene, clean, clear state of mind. Bhagavan says thats not how it works, and therefore you shouldnt be desirous of clinging to those states. Many people say, I was meditating, the very first day it was very good, but from the second day onward nothing really happened.
The more you desire and grasp, the more it will stay away from you. In Gujarat there is a saying: one who is asking for it, things go away from them; and one who says I dont need it, people will come to you. The more you say I dont need it, the more people offer; the more you say I want it, the more people take away from you. So Bhagavan says, when the effects of these three gunas are present, dont hate them. Understand that these are the common experiences for everyone. Na nivrittani -- when something is absent, when I was enjoying my activity, I was very busy, and now Im not -- accept it as is.
So the acceptance is the mark of a true Gnani. One who accepts his reality as it is -- that is Bhagavans answer to Arjunas question: what are his qualities? His qualities are that he accepts things as they are. He does not hate them if they are happening; he does not desire them if they are not happening. Now this is very difficult for us to accept, because as soon as we talk about somebody, we say, I dont know, he has been talking about all this, but then the other day this thing happened and he reacted this way. He reacted this way because this is how he was made up through all his life.
But you do not know how that incident affected him. Once, at the core of your being, you become a witness.

Krishnas answer to Arjunas question is revolutionary and often misunderstood. Verse 22 does NOT say the gunas disappear for the enlightened one. Rather: prakāsham cha pravrittim cha moham eva cha... na dveshti sampravrittāni na nivrittāni kānkshati, when light (Sattva), activity (Rajas), or delusion (Tamas) are present, he does not hate them; when they are absent, he does not crave them. This is radical acceptance. The liberated one still experiences all three gunas, clarity fades into restlessness, restlessness into dullness, but he neither clings to the pleasant states nor pushes away the unpleasant ones. He remains udāsīnavat āsīnah, seated like one indifferent, unmoved by the gunas play.
Verse 24 paints the portrait of such equanimity: sama-duhkha-sukhah svastah, equal in pain and pleasure, established in the Self. Sama-loshta-ashma-kānchanah, to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same. Tulya-priya-apriyah, equal toward the pleasant and unpleasant. Tulya-nindā-ātma-samstutih, the same whether criticized or praised. This is not suppression or indifference but a fundamental shift in identity. Today, test yourself: When you are in a sattvic, clear state, do you grasp at it, fearing its loss? When you feel dull or agitated, do you fight against it? Practice letting each state arise and pass without the second layer of reaction, without craving the good or hating the bad. Notice: the one who can observe both pleasant and unpleasant states with equanimity is already beyond both. That witness is your true nature.
